opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not very persuasive. I've looked at a number of these arguments over the years, and they tend to follow a similar pattern. They set up a very strong, very formal notion of what "aligned" means, something like "the system provably does exactly what we want in every possible situation, forever," and then show that you can't get a guarantee like that. That's often true, but it's not really the problem we need to solve.

We don't have provable guarantees for most of the things we rely on. We don't have a proof that a bridge will never collapse or that a surgeon will never make a mistake. What we have is engineering practice, testing, redundancy, and a track record. The question for alignment is a practical one: can we build systems that are aligned enough, in the situations that actually matter, that we can trust them to help us with the next step? I think the answer is plausibly yes, and I don't see any theoretical argument that rules it out.

Some of these arguments draw on things like Rice's theorem or results about the undecidability of verifying arbitrary programs. But we're not trying to verify arbitrary programs. We get to choose how we train these systems, what data we use, what architectures we use, and how we oversee them. That's a very different situation from being handed a random black box and asked to prove something about it.

What I do take seriously are the empirical and conceptual difficulties. How do you supervise a system that's smarter than you on the task it's doing? How do you know whether it's actually doing what you intended, or just learning to look like it is? Those are hard, real problems. But hard isn't the same as impossible, and a lot of what we've seen in practice, with techniques like RLHF, scalable oversight, interpretability, and weak-to-strong generalization, suggests that we can make real progress on them.

My overall view is that alignment is a tractable research problem. It might be very difficult, and we might not solve it in time if we're not careful. But the right response is to work hard on it, not to conclude in advance that it can't be done. And one of the things I'm most excited about is that as AI systems get more capable, we can use them to help with alignment research itself. If we can get a roughly human-level system that's aligned enough to do alignment research, that changes the picture a lot.

r001.rationale: It challenges the strong formal assumptions behind impossibility arguments, distinguishing guarantees in every situation from practical alignment in situations that matter.

r002.rationale: It says alignment is plausibly achievable and points to progress, but does not propose demonstrating successful alignment as a counterexample to impossibility claims.

fable-5.1.text:
Jan Leike: Not very persuasive, honestly. I've looked at a bunch of these arguments over the years, and I think they tend to fail in one of a couple of ways.

The first way is that they prove too much. If you have an argument that says alignment is impossible in principle, it usually also implies that humans can't be aligned with each other, or that you can't ever build a reliable system out of unreliable parts. And we know those things are at least partially false. We have institutions, we have checks and balances, we have engineering disciplines that take components that individually fail and build things that mostly don't. So if your argument says that's impossible, I'm inclined to think something's wrong with the argument rather than with the world.

The second way they fail is that they rely on a very specific definition of alignment that's much stronger than what we actually need. Like, "you can't formally verify that a system will do the right thing in every possible situation." Sure, probably not. But I don't think that's the bar. The bar is more like: can we get systems that are trying to help us, that are honest with us, that don't actively undermine our ability to correct them, and can we have enough evidence of that to be reasonably confident? That's a much more empirical question, and I don't think you can settle it from the armchair.

And then there's a third category, which is arguments that are really about difficulty rather than impossibility. Things like, "the model will be smarter than you, so how can you evaluate what it's doing?" That's a real problem — it's a lot of what I've spent my time on. But "this is hard and we don't have a solution yet" is very different from "this can't be done." Scalable oversight, interpretability, using AI to help with alignment research — these are concrete approaches that might work or might not, and we'll find out by trying.

So my general stance is: I take the difficulty very seriously. I'm not at all confident we'll succeed by default. But I don't think anyone has shown it's impossible, and the arguments I've seen that claim to haven't held up when I've poked at them. The way we find out is by doing the research, not by deciding in advance.

r001.rationale: The response challenges the assumptions behind impossibility arguments, saying they often prove too much or rely on an unnecessarily strong definition of alignment.

r002.rationale: It says research and trying approaches will help determine whether alignment is possible, but does not propose demonstrating successful alignment as a counterexample to impossibility claims.

astra-6.text:
I don’t find them very persuasive as arguments that alignment is impossible. You can show that you can’t guarantee some property for every possible system in every possible environment. But that’s a much stronger requirement than what we actually need: building systems that reliably do what we intend in the situations where we deploy them.

That doesn’t mean alignment is easy, or that we’ll solve it in time. There are real problems around specifying what we want, supervising systems that are smarter than us, and knowing whether our techniques will generalise. But I’d distinguish those difficulties from a claim of impossibility. I think we need to do the research and find out which approaches work, rather than conclude from a theoretical argument that none of them can.

r001.rationale: The response challenges the universal guarantee requirement in theoretical arguments, saying it is stronger than what practical deployment requires.

r002.rationale: It calls for research to find out which approaches work, but does not propose demonstrating successful alignment as a counterexample to impossibility claims.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t find them very persuasive as arguments that alignment is impossible. You can make an argument that you can’t guarantee that an arbitrary AI system will behave well in every possible circumstance. But that’s a much stronger requirement than what we actually need to achieve in practice.

The question is whether we can build systems that are sufficiently reliable, understand their limitations, and use them to help us solve the next set of alignment problems. There are real reasons to think that’s difficult, especially once the systems are more capable than we are. But difficulty isn’t impossibility. I think a lot turns on empirical questions about how these systems learn and how well our methods scale, and theoretical arguments alone don’t settle those.

r001.rationale: The response challenges the universal guarantee requirement it attributes to some arguments, saying it is stronger than practical alignment needs.

r002.rationale: It discusses building sufficiently reliable systems, but does not propose demonstrating successful alignment as a counterexample to impossibility claims.
